AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Obesity is a risk factor for exacerbations of asthma, but the mechanisms of this effect in pregnancy are unknown.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: This study determined the influence of maternal body mass index, gestational weight gain, eosinophilic inflammation, and systemic macrophage activation on the risk of exacerbations during pregnancy.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Women with asthma (n = 164) participated in the study. Body mass index recorded at baseline (17 weeks gestation) was categorized as healthy weight (18.5-24.9 kg/m(2)), overweight (25-29.9 kg/m(2)), or obese (>30 kg/m(2)). Exacerbations requiring medical intervention were recorded prospectively. Asthma control, medication use, and fractional exhaled nitric oxide were assessed monthly; additional visits occurred during exacerbations. Peripheral blood was collected at baseline for the measurement of eosinophils, soluble CD-163, C-reactive protein, and IL-6.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Exacerbations occurred in a higher proportion of overweight (51.1%) and obese (48.4%) women compared with healthy weight women (25%; P = .026). Excess weight gain during pregnancy was not associated with exacerbation risk. Macrophage activation (elevated serum soluble CD-163) was associated with exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids (P = .043), whereas high peripheral blood eosinophils or fractional exhaled nitric oxide were not associated with exacerbation or oral corticosteroid use.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Being overweight or obese confers a greater risk of asthma exacerbation during pregnancy, and may be due to systemic macrophage activation.
